name: Capromorelin
lead: Capromorelin is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist and growth hormone secretagogue developed by Pfizer. Ghrelin is the hormone that signals hunger and stimulates growth hormone release, so capromorelin drives appetite and raises growth hormone and IGF-1 levels [1]. It is approved for veterinary use, as Entyce for appetite stimulation in dogs (US, 2016) and Elura for weight loss in cats with chronic kidney disease (US, 2020) [1][2].

The appearance connection is through body composition. Growth hormone secretagogues are discussed in physique and anti-ageing communities as a way to raise growth hormone and add lean mass, and capromorelin was tested for that purpose in older adults: in a year-long trial in people aged 65-84, recipients gained about 1.4 kg of lean mass over six months [1][4]. Development for people was discontinued, and no study has examined capromorelin for cosmetic purposes in healthy adults.
Today it exists as a veterinary prescription drug, and its human literature consists of the older-adult trial and early-phase safety and pharmacokinetic work [4][9].
infobox: Veterinary prescription drug; not approved for humans [1]

paras: In dogs, capromorelin is indicated for appetite stimulation (US approval May 2016, as Entyce), and in cats for weight loss associated with chronic kidney disease (US approval October 2020, as Elura) [1][2]. Wikipedia describes Elura as the second drug approved for weight loss in cats and the first for cats with that condition, and notes that the European Union's product is Eluracat, with its public assessment report dated May 2023 [1]. A veterinary review describes capromorelin as a novel therapy for stimulating appetite in dogs [6].

Capromorelin binds the growth hormone secretagogue receptor 1a with high affinity (Ki 7 nM in the original discovery work) and stimulated growth hormone release in rat pituitary cells [5]. It mimics ghrelin's action on the hypothalamus and pituitary, producing a pulse of growth hormone secretion similar in pattern to that of puberty and young adulthood, and raising growth hormone and IGF-1 levels [1]. Because ghrelin also stimulates feeding, the same receptor action explains the appetite effect used in veterinary medicine. In mice, a comparison with ghrelin and GHRP-6 examined effects on gastric emptying [7].

Capromorelin is orally absorbed. Medicinal chemistry papers report analogues designed for longer half-lives, and a single-ascending-dose phase 1 trial in people with spinal cord injury and able-bodied volunteers examined its pharmacokinetics.[8][9]
Capromorelin is a pyrazolinone-piperidine dipeptide mimetic, with molecular formula C28H35N5O4 and a molar mass of about 505.6 g/mol.[1][5]

In animals, reported side effects on the veterinary product include vomiting and diarrhoea (Grokipedia, AI-generated).[10] Human safety data come from the early-phase and older-adult studies described below.[4][9]

A randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled multicentre study examined the oral secretagogue in older adults with mild functional limitation, looking at hormonal, body composition and performance effects [4]. Wikipedia summarises the trial, which began in 1999 and enrolled 395 adults aged 65 to 84, as showing an average gain of about 1.4 kg (3 lb) of lean mass in the first six months and improvement on a straight-line walking test of balance, strength and coordination, with stair climbing improving by 12 months. The results were not judged strong enough to continue into a planned second year, and human studies had been discontinued by 2017 [1].

A phase 1 single-ascending-dose study assessed pharmacokinetics and safety in spinal cord-injured and able-bodied volunteers, and rodent work examined its effect on defecation after spinal cord injury [9][11]. A systematic review of drugs for frailty includes growth hormone secretagogue trials in its coverage [12]. No trial has tested capromorelin for appearance goals in healthy adults.

Pfizer researchers published the discovery of capromorelin (code CP-424,391) in 2002-2003, describing it as a pyrazolinone-piperidine dipeptide mimetic and publishing analogues designed for longer half-lives [5][8][13]. The human program ran from 1999 and ended after the older-adult trial [1]. The compound was later developed for companion animals, reaching the US market for dogs in 2016 and cats in 2020 [1][6].

Capromorelin belongs to the same class as other oral growth hormone secretagogues, which appear in physique and anti-ageing discussions as non-injectable ways to raise growth hormone. Its only marketed forms are veterinary products, and it is not approved for human use [1].

card.summary: Oral ghrelin agonist sold as a pet appetite stimulant; a human older-adult trial showed modest lean mass change and was not pursued.
card.note: Veterinary product; not approved for humans.

quick.overview:
Capromorelin is a Pfizer-developed drug that mimics ghrelin. It is sold for pets as Entyce (dogs) and Elura (cats with kidney disease).

In people, a trial in older adults reported a small lean-mass gain, but development in humans was discontinued. No study has tested it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It activates the ghrelin/GH secretagogue receptor, raising appetite and growth hormone and IGF-1 levels.
quick.risks: It is a veterinary prescription drug, with vomiting and diarrhoea noted in animals. Human safety data are limited to early-phase and older-adult trials.

chain: Raises growth hormone and IGF-1 and stimulates appetite
Older-adult trial reported a gain in lean body mass
angle.text: Capromorelin acts like ghrelin to increase growth hormone and appetite. In the one trial in people it was tested for body composition in older adults, which is the basis for interest in it as a lean-mass compound.
